Abstract
Blockchain technology offers a robust framework for integration with the Internet of 
Things (IoT), enhancing interoperability, security, privacy, and scalability in mod-
ern technological ecosystems. However, traditional cryptographic protocols used in 
blockchain systems are increasingly vulnerable to quantum attacks due to advance-
ments in quantum computing. In response, the National Institute of Standards and 
Technology (NIST) has prioritized research in post-quantum cryptography, pre-
senting challenges and opportunities for developing blockchain-based applications 
tailored to IoT devices. Among the post-quantum cryptographic schemes evaluated 
in NIST’s third standardization round, the Supersingular Isogeny Key Encapsula-
tion (SIKE) protocol stands out for its relatively small public and private key sizes. 
Despite this advantage, SIKE faces challenges related to high latency, necessitating 
efficient implementations to make it viable for real-world applications. This research 
focuses on optimizing the cryptographic foundations of blockchain networks to 
securely and efficiently integrate resource-constrained IoT ecosystems. By enhanc-
ing the SIKE protocol, which exhibits strong resistance to brute-force and white-
washing attacks, the study achieves significant performance improvements. Our 
FPGA-based implementation on the VIRTEX-6 XC6VLX760 demonstrates reduced 
latency, achieving a key generation time of 24 ms, encapsulation time of 72 ms, and 
decapsulation time of 73 ms for SIKEp434. These results highlight the feasibility of 
deploying SIKE-optimized blockchain networks in IoT environments with stringent 
resource constraints.

1  Introduction
The advent of quantum computing has significantly shifted research focus toward 
developing cryptographic algorithms resilient to quantum attacks. Classical cryp-
tographic techniques, such as Rivest–Shamir–Adleman (RSA) and Elliptic Curve 
Cryptography (ECC), are vulnerable to quantum computers because they can effi-
ciently solve problems like integer factorization and discrete logarithms [1, 2]. This 
poses a severe threat to the security of blockchain-based applications [3, 4], neces-
sitating the transition to cryptographic protocols capable of withstanding quantum 
computing capabilities [5].
To address these vulnerabilities, researchers have focused on post-quantum cryp-
tography (PQC), which aims to maintain current security levels while resisting the 
computational power of quantum computers [5]. Figure 1 presents a comprehensive

ported research into five distinct PQC methods, including those based on supersin-
gular elliptic curve isogenies, to advance post-quantum security and privacy [15]. 
However, implementing these cryptographic primitives in IoT environments pre-
sents unique challenges [16], such as:
•	 Resource Constraints: Limited memory, storage, and processing power.
•	 Energy Efficiency: Optimizing battery life and power consumption.
•	 Scalability: Managing large numbers of heterogeneous IoT devices and ensuring 
interoperability.
•	 Real-Time Constraints: Addressing latency and throughput for time-sensitive 
applications.
•	 Key Management: Efficiently managing key distribution, storage, and updates.
•	 Physical Security: Ensuring tamper resistance and secure firmware updates.
•	 Privacy: Protecting data confidentiality and user privacy.
Blockchain networks integrated into IoT systems face additional challenges, 
including scalability limitations, transaction latency, and protocol standardization 
[17]. Techniques such as sharding, off-chain transactions, and lightweight consensus 
mechanisms are critical for addressing scalability [18], while middleware solutions 
and standardized protocols can improve interoperability [21]. Addressing these chal-
lenges requires combining lightweight cryptographic algorithms, efficient key man-
agement, robust hardware security, and adherence to emerging IoT security stand-
ards [20]. Furthermore, the dynamic and heterogeneous nature of IoT environments 
necessitates cryptographic primitives that are flexible and adaptable to evolving 
security needs. Figure 3a and b illustrates these challenges, highlighting the barriers 
to secure IoT integration and blockchain adoption in IoT applications.

1.1  Benefits of SIKE for blockchain‑based resource‑constrained IoT
Blockchain is a transformative distributed ledger technology that employs cryp-
tographic techniques, such as public key cryptography and hashing functions, to 
ensure secure data transmission between nodes and reliable data storage. These 
mechanisms provide robust security and data integrity. However, quantum com-
puters, leveraging Shor’s algorithm, pose a significant threat to the security of 
both symmetric and asymmetric cryptographic keys, including public key sys-
tems, as illustrated in Fig. 4 [14, 20, 21].
Supersingular Isogeny Key Encapsulation (SIKE), a post-quantum crypto-
graphic algorithm recognized in NIST’s standardization efforts, offers a promis-
ing solution to this challenge [15]. Based on elliptic curve cryptography (ECC), 
which is a cornerstone of modern blockchain architectures, SIKE provides 
enhanced quantum resistance [19, 22]. Its implementation demonstrates advan-
tages in resource-constrained environments, such as Field-Programmable Gate 
Arrays (FPGAs), where its efficient use of computational resources and optimized 
performance in terms of area and speed make it highly suitable.
SIKE’s cryptosystem can be effectively integrated into various stages of block-
chain systems to address quantum vulnerabilities. Applications include:
•	 Node and User Identification: Ensuring secure authentication within the 
blockchain network.
•	 Transaction Security: Safeguarding communications during transactions.
•	 Data Integrity: Leveraging SIKE’s secure hashing techniques to protect 
stored data.
These capabilities highlight SIKE as a critical enabler for building secure, 
efficient, and scalable blockchain networks tailored to resource-constrained IoT 
ecosystems.

1.2  Blockchain for IoT security and privacy
The foundation of this research is based on the robust principles of post-quantum 
cryptographic (PQC) Key Encapsulation Mechanisms (KEMs), which extend the 
traditional two-party Diffie–Hellman key exchange. SIKE, an isogeny-based KEM, 
provides a high level of security against quantum adversaries by leveraging the com-
putational difficulty of finding isogenies between supersingular elliptic curves. Its 
flexible structure facilitates easy conversion between KEMs and Public Key Encryp-
tion (PKE) schemes, making it adaptable for various Blockchain-IoT applications. 
Integrating SIKE into blockchain operations ensures secure key exchanges for IoT 
devices and enables lightweight signatures for transaction authentication. Addi-
tionally, this study examines the Number Theoretic Transform (NTT), which is

1.3  Motivation and objectives
The implementation of Supersingular Isogeny Key Encapsulation (SIKE) for block-
chain-based, resource-constrained IoT ecosystems is driven by several key factors:
•	 Quantum Computing Threats: Traditional cryptographic algorithms, such as 
RSA and ECC, are increasingly vulnerable to the growing power of quantum 
computing. SIKE, as a post-quantum cryptographic algorithm, provides robust 
protection against these threats, ensuring the long-term security of IoT and 
blockchain systems.
•	 IoT Device Resource Constraints: IoT devices often operate under strict 
resource limitations, including constrained memory, processing power, and 
energy supply. SIKE’s design prioritizes efficiency, reducing computational 
demands and minimizing energy consumption, making it an ideal solution for 
battery-powered IoT devices.
•	 Smaller Key Sizes and Bandwidth Efficiency: SIKE’s smaller key sizes and 
ciphertexts are advantageous in bandwidth-constrained environments, reducing 
transmission latency and enhancing system performance. These compact crypto-
graphic elements also require less storage, addressing the storage limitations of 
IoT devices.
•	 Secure and Scalable IoT Solutions: IoT devices are frequent targets of cyberat-
tacks. SIKE significantly improves the security of communication and data stor-
age within IoT ecosystems while supporting the scalability of networks as the 
number of connected devices grows.
•	 Blockchain Integration Benefits: Blockchain relies on cryptographic algo-
rithms to secure transactions and ensure data integrity. By incorporating SIKE, 
blockchain systems maintain resilience against quantum computing advances, 
ensuring the integrity and confidentiality of IoT data transmissions and storage.

2  Literature review
The potential application of post-quantum cryptography (PQC) in IoT environments 
has garnered significant attention in recent years. Numerous studies have analyzed 
various PQC schemes, including Supersingular Isogeny Key Encapsulation (SIKE), 
to evaluate their suitability for resource-constrained IoT use cases [4, 25–28].
2.1  Post‑quantum cryptography for IoT
Several works compare PQC algorithms to assess their performance on IoT devices. 
For instance, [30] provides a comprehensive evaluation of multiple PQC schemes, 
outlining the benefits and limitations of implementing SIKE on constrained devices. 
The findings in [28–32] highlight the efficiency of SIKE in terms of smaller key 
sizes, lower bandwidth requirements, and reduced computational overhead, which 
are crucial for IoT systems with limited resources.
2.2  Blockchain‑based security for IoT
Studies exploring blockchain-based security solutions for IoT [18, 20, 33] emphasize 
the integration of PQC, including SIKE, as a proactive measure to mitigate future 
quantum threats. These works demonstrate how blockchain technology can enhance 
IoT security by decentralizing trust and providing secure, immutable records. They 
also detail the challenges and trade-offs involved in implementing PQC within 
blockchain frameworks for IoT environments.
2.3  Established benchmarks for blockchain in IoT
Various established benchmarks have been proposed to develop blockchain plat-
forms that effectively address the centralization problem in IoT applications while 
improving security across all layers. For example, the work in [34–36] focused on 
building blockchain platforms to secure communication among IoT components. 
These platforms utilized elliptic curve cryptography (ECC) protocols and imple-
mented Practical Byzantine Fault Tolerance (PBFT) as the consensus algorithm. A

3  Framework for SIKE implementation
Implementing the Supersingular Isogeny Key Encapsulation (SIKE) protocol in

straints of IoT devices and the computational demands of blockchain operations.

•	 Compact Key Management: Leveraging SIKE’s smaller key sizes compared to 
other PQC schemes, enabling seamless deployment on IoT devices with con-
strained memory.
•	 Quantum-Resilient Security: Ensuring that IoT sensor data and cryptographic 
operations remain secure against quantum adversaries.
•	 Blockchain Integration: Demonstrating the application of SIKE to establish 
secure, immutable logging of IoT data within a distributed ledger.

4.1  Mathematics of the SIKE PROTOCOL
The SIKE protocol involves three primary phases for secure communication 
between Alice and Bob [57]:
•	 p434-Key Generation (KeyGen): Both parties generate their respective private 
and public keys.
•	 p434-Key Encapsulation (Encap): Alice or Bob encapsulates a shared secret 
into a ciphertext that can only be decapsulated by the intended recipient.
•	 p434-Key Decapsulation (Decap): The recipient decapsulates the ciphertext to 
derive the shared secret.
These phases rely on the underlying SIDH (Supersingular Isogeny Diffie-Hell-
man) protocol, which provides the foundational mathematical operations required 
for SIKE. The SIDH protocol operates within a prime field and leverages elliptic 
curve isogenies to generate the shared secret.
4.1.1  Key generation, encapsulation, and decapsulation
The SIDH process forms the backbone of SIKE and comprises the following steps 
(illustrated in Fig. 8):
Step 1. Selection of a prime field, tailored for secure isogeny-based operations.
Step 2. Execution of elliptic curve operations, including isogeny generation, ker-
nel computation, and point multiplication.
Step 3. Sharing and processing of public parameters to ensure secure exchange.
Building on SIDH, the SIKE protocol introduces additional encapsulation 
and decapsulation steps using the SHAKE256 cryptographic hash function. 
The SHAKE256 function ensures the integrity of the encapsulated key during 
transmission.
4.1.2  Key establishment process
The key establishment process between Alice and Bob, shown in Fig. 9, proceeds as 
follows:
•	 Key Generation: Both Alice and Bob compute their private and public keys 
using the SIDH protocol.
•	 Parameter Exchange: Public parameters are exchanged between Alice and Bob.
•	 Encapsulation: One party (e.g., Alice) encapsulates a secret key and transmits 
the ciphertext to the other party (e.g., Bob).
•	 Decapsulation: The recipient (Bob) decapsulates the ciphertext to derive the 
shared secret.

7  Conclusion
Implementing SIKE (Supersingular Isogeny Key Encapsulation) on FPGAs for 
blockchain-based resource-constrained IoT devices requires a comprehensive 
approach that involves architectural planning, optimization strategies, and taking 
advantage of FPGA-specific features like parallelism and pipelining. By leveraging 
industry-standard tools and studying key research papers, substantial performance 
improvements and energy efficiency can be achieved. The existing literature on 
SIKE for blockchain-based IoT has explored various theoretical frameworks, practi-
cal implementations, and applications that highlight its potential to enhance secu-
rity and performance in IoT environments—particularly in light of quantum com-
puting threats.
Through this paper, we demonstrate that SIKE offers a robust post-quantum 
cryptography solution to address the vulnerabilities IoT devices face in the future 
with quantum computers. However, while SIKE shows great promise, implement-
ing it on resource-constrained devices like those typically used in IoT requires 
careful attention to computational and energy constraints as depicted in Fig. 12. 
Ongoing research is necessary to further optimize SIKE’s performance and make 
it scalable for use in various IoT and blockchain scenarios. FPGAs offer significant 
advantages in performance and energy efficiency, which make them an excellent 
platform for implementing SIKE in resource-constrained environments. Through 
careful architecture design, the use of optimization techniques, and exploiting the 
parallelism inherent in FPGAs, SIKE can be efficiently integrated into IoT systems 
to provide quantum-resistant security. As IoT environments evolve, the need for 
enhanced security, efficiency, scalability, and adherence to future-proof crypto-
graphic standards becomes increasingly urgent. SIKE, with its potential to address 
these challenges, stands out as a forward-looking solution to secure the growing IoT 
ecosystem. Its deployment in blockchain-based IoT environments offers a robust 
defense against quantum threats, while also meeting the stringent demands of IoT 
devices, which often operate with limited resources. In conclusion, SIKE’s integra-
tion into blockchain-based IoT ecosystems addresses unique security challenges, 
offering a promising solution for both the present and future needs of IoT secu-
rity, especially as the industry prepares for the rise of quantum computing threats.

numerous devices.

Abstract: Blockchain technology offers a robust framework for integration with the Internet of Things (IoT), enhancing interoperability, security, privacy, and scalability in mod- ern technological ecosystems. However, traditional cryptographic protocols used in blockchain systems are increasingly vulnerable to quantum attacks due to advance- ments in quantum computing. In response, the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) has prioritized research in post-quantum cryptography, pre- senting challenges and opportunities for developing blockchain-based applications tailored to IoT devices. Among the post-quantum cryptographic schemes evaluated in NIST’s third standardization round, the Supersingular Isogeny Key Encapsula- tion (SIKE) protocol stands out for its relatively small public and private key sizes. Despite this advantage, SIKE faces challenges related to high latency, necessitating efficient implementations to make it viable for real-world applications. This research focuses on optimizing the cryptographic foundations of blockchain networks to securely and efficiently integrate resource-constrained IoT ecosystems. By enhanc- ing the SIKE protocol, which exhibits strong resistance to brute-force and white- washing attacks, the study achieves significant performance improvements. Our FPGA-based implementation on the VIRTEX-6 XC6VLX760 demonstrates reduced latency, achieving a key generation time of 24 ms, encapsulation time of 72 ms, and decapsulation time of 73 ms for SIKEp434. These results highlight the feasibility of deploying SIKE-optimized blockchain networks in IoT environments with stringent resource constraints.
